candidates.name: MAP1S-brake release
candidates.biological_hypothesis: The proximal consequence of CDKL5 loss is persistent, unphosphorylated MAP1S binding to dendritic microtubules, producing over-long microtubule growth episodes and impaired dendritic cargo transport. Lowering MAP1S dose (or otherwise reducing its microtubule-binding occupancy) should restore normal microtubule dynamics and, downstream, dendritic arborization and synapse maturation, without needing CDKL5 kinase activity.
candidates.target_or_process: MAP1S (and more broadly the CDKL5-substrate node MAP1S/EB2/ARHGEF2 controlling dendritic microtubule dynamics and cargo transport)
candidates.desired_perturbation: Partial reduction of MAP1S protein level or of its microtubule association in forebrain neurons; normalization of microtubule growth-episode length and dendritic transport

evidence_for.statement: Lowering MAP1S levels rescued abnormal microtubule dynamics in Cdkl5 knockout neurons — a direct rescue experiment identifying MAP1S as the mediator of a core cellular phenotype.
Two independent phosphoproteomic studies converge on microtubule regulators as the physiological CDKL5 substrates, making this node the best-supported proximal mechanism.
Because the rescue is downstream of the kinase, it is genotype-agnostic: it should work for deletions, truncating, splice and missense variants alike.
Phospho-EB2 is a measurable readout of CDKL5 pathway activity in vivo, usable as a pharmacodynamic/engagement assay for screening modifiers of this node.

CNS-delivered oligonucleotides that reduce a target transcript are an established, clinically validated modality for neurodevelopmental/epileptic disorders (intrathecal ASO precedents), so a MAP1S-lowering ASO is a realistic implementation.

evidence_against.statement: The rescue demonstrated is of a cell-biological phenotype (microtubule dynamics), not of seizures, cognition or visual deficits; no evidence retrieved that MAP1S lowering improves any animal-level phenotype.

MAP1S has roles outside the CDKL5 pathway (autophagy, mitotic/cytoskeletal functions); chronic systemic or CNS-wide knockdown could carry its own toxicity, and the therapeutic window for partial lowering is unknown.

candidates.key_biological_uncertainty: Does normalizing microtubule dynamics by MAP1S lowering translate into improvement of dendritic arborization and any behavioural/EEG phenotype in Cdkl5 knockout animals, and is there a postnatal window in which it still works? This single in vivo experiment (CNS MAP1S ASO or conditional Map1s reduction in Cdkl5-null mice, with phospho-EB2-independent readouts: dendritic morphology, visual evoked potentials, convulsant-threshold EEG) is the decisive de-risking step.

candidates.name: Genotype-stratified CDKL5 output boost
candidates.biological_hypothesis: CDD is a dose-sensitive loss-of-function disorder, so any intervention that increases the amount of catalytically competent CDKL5 protein from the patient's own alleles should be beneficial. This is one biology (raise functional CDKL5 protein) with variant-class-specific implementations: splice-correcting ASOs for splice-site/pseudoexon variants, translational readthrough or NMD modulation for nonsense variants, and stabilizing/chaperone-like small molecules for hypomorphic missense kinase-domain variants with residual folding capacity.
candidates.target_or_process: CDKL5 pre-mRNA processing, mRNA surveillance (NMD) and mutant kinase protein stability
candidates.desired_perturbation: Increase functional CDKL5 protein above the disease threshold; measurable as restored phosphorylation of EB2/MAP1S

evidence_for.statement: CDD is monogenic loss of function of CDKL5, and variant classes include splice and truncating as well as missense variants concentrated in the catalytic domain — i.e. a substantial fraction of patients have alleles amenable to splice correction, readthrough or stabilization rather than needing whole-gene replacement.

Restoring CDKL5 protein to the mouse brain increases EB2 phosphorylation, confirming that added CDKL5 protein is functional in vivo and providing a direct, quantitative success criterion for any output-boosting agent.

Splice-modulating and poison-exon ASOs that raise the output of a haploinsufficient neuronal gene are clinically validated (nusinersen) and in development for epileptic encephalopathies, including a patient-specific splice ASO for an ultra-rare variant — so the regulatory and delivery path for an n-of-few CDKL5 splice ASO exists.

Because heterozygous females are mosaic for X-inactivation, even a modest increase in output from the active mutant allele in affected cells could shift many cells above threshold; this makes partial restoration potentially meaningful rather than all-or-nothing.

evidence_against.statement: Whether missense kinase-domain variants retain residual or instead act dominant-negatively is unresolved; if dominant-negative, stabilizing the mutant protein could be harmful rather than helpful.
No CDKL5-specific splice-correcting, readthrough or protein-stabilizing agent was identified in the retrieved literature; this is an unstarted discovery program, not a repurposing opportunity.
Each implementation serves only a small variant subset of an already ultra-rare disease (deletions are not addressable at all), which severely limits the addressable population per agent.

candidates.key_biological_uncertainty: What fraction of CDKL5 variants are actually output-limited rather than null, and how much protein is enough? The enabling work is a variant-function catalogue: express patient missense/splice alleles in neurons and measure phospho-EB2 to classify each as null, hypomorphic or dominant-negative, and to define the restoration threshold. Note: reactivating the silent wild-type X allele would address the same biology but is epigenome editing and therefore out of scope for this team.

candidates.name: E/I-rebalance for the encephalopathy
candidates.biological_hypothesis: The most disabling features — infancy-onset refractory seizures and developmental arrest — may be driven not by the microtubule defect per se but by a cell-type-specific excitation/inhibition imbalance arising from impaired dendritic/synaptic maturation in forebrain glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons. If so, interventions that correct network excitability or restore synaptic maturation signalling (e.g. the altered Akt/rpS6 axis) could reduce seizures and improve cortical function without touching CDKL5 or its substrates.
candidates.target_or_process: Forebrain excitatory/inhibitory synaptic balance and the Akt/rpS6 synaptic-maturation signalling axis
candidates.desired_perturbation: Reduce cortical/hippocampal network hyperexcitability and restore normal synaptic maturation signalling; readout = convulsant-threshold EEG, visual evoked potentials, dendritic/synaptic morphology

evidence_for.statement: Cdkl5 knockout mice show abnormal EEG responses to convulsants, reduced visual evoked responses, reduced dendritic arborization and altered Akt/rpS6 signalling, and distinct behaviours map to excitatory versus inhibitory forebrain neurons — establishing a cell-type-resolved circuit phenotype and quantitative endpoints.

Because synapse maturation and seizures are downstream of the substrate defect, this route is genotype-agnostic and, unlike the proximal routes, can use existing CNS-penetrant small molecules, giving the shortest path to a testable clinical hypothesis.

evidence_against.statement: The causal chain from lost substrate phosphorylation to epilepsy is not established — this is the field's central gap, so the target of an E/I-rebalancing agent cannot currently be specified mechanistically.

Knockout mice do not have spontaneous seizures, only altered convulsant sensitivity, so the primary clinical endpoint (refractory infantile seizures) cannot be modelled in the standard mouse — an anti-seizure efficacy claim is not testable in that model.

Patients' seizures are by definition pharmacoresistant to existing broad anti-seizure medicines, which argues that generic excitability reduction is insufficient and that a CDD-specific circuit mechanism must be found first.

candidates.key_biological_uncertainty: Which neuron subtype and which developmental window generate the epileptic phenotype, and is there any model that shows spontaneous CDD-like seizures? Without a seizure-competent model (patient-derived neuronal networks/organoids, rat or conditional cell-type-specific models) this hypothesis is not yet testable for its most important endpoint, even though the visual-evoked-potential and dendritic endpoints are testable now.

conclusion_note: The cause is certain (CDKL5 loss of function) and the proximal substrate biology is validated (PMID:30266824, PMID:30377159), so hypothesis 1 (MAP1S-brake release) rests on real rescue evidence and is the best-supported starting point. However, the chain from lost substrate phosphorylation to epilepsy is unestablished, and the standard knockout mouse lacks spontaneous seizures (PMID:24838000) — so for the dominant clinical endpoint this verges on NO ADEQUATE MODEL, and hypothesis 3 should be treated as not yet testable for seizures. Two gating experiments would reshape all three: (a) does postnatal MAP1S lowering rescue animal-level phenotypes, and (b) is any deficit reversible after symptom onset (no evidence retrieved either way — absence of literature here is not evidence against). Hypothesis 2 additionally requires a variant-function catalogue using phospho-EB2 (PMID:39033321) before any missense-stabilization work, since dominant-negative behaviour would invert the strategy. Caveats: targeted searches for CDD-specific pharmacological rescue returned off-target results and some earlier searches hit rate limits, so agent-level coverage is incomplete and NO EXISTING AGENT IDENTIFIED may apply to hypotheses 1 and 2 on fuller searching.
